# Extract Term-Level Contributions

A GAM prediction is an intercept plus a sum of smooth functions. `predict(type="terms")` exposes
each smooth's contribution separately, so you can see how much each predictor is adding to the
linear predictor at any covariate value. This is useful for explaining which variable is driving a
high or low fitted value.

## Fit

Fit a two-smooth Gaussian GAM on the wages dataset.

::: {#c1037293 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import whittaker as wk
import numpy as np

data = wk.load_dataset("wages")
model = wk.GAM("wage ~ s(age) + s(experience)").fit(data)
model.summary()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1}

## Extract term contributions

Pass `type="terms"` to `predict()`. The return type is `TermsPredictionResult` with a `.terms`
dict and a `.labels` list.

::: {#1c43162f .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
new_data = {"age": np.array([25, 35, 45, 55]), "experience": np.array([2, 10, 18, 28])}
preds_terms = model.predict(new_data, type="terms")
preds_terms.labels
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2}
```
['s(age)', 's(experience)']
```
:::
:::


The labels show the exact term names used as keys in `.terms` (they match the formula notation).

## Inspect each smooth's contribution

Access each term's contribution array using its label.

::: {#fc533bdc .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
preds_terms.terms["s(age)"].round(3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3}
```
array([-21.521,  -9.109,   5.311,  14.86 ])
```
:::
:::


::: {#9553a329 .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
preds_terms.terms["s(experience)"].round(3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4}
```
array([-4.84 ,  4.884, 12.297, 15.613])
```
:::
:::


Each value is the smooth's contribution to the linear predictor at the corresponding row in
`new_data`, centered so that it integrates to zero over the data. A large positive value means
that covariate value pushes the prediction upward.

## Sum of contributions

The `.values` property sums all term contributions, giving the linear predictor minus the
intercept.

::: {#0bde0a28 .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
preds_terms.values.round(3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5}
```
array([-26.361,  -4.225,  17.608,  30.473])
```
:::
:::


To compare with the full link-scale prediction (which adds the intercept), call `predict()` with
`type="link"`.

::: {#2da0207c .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
link_preds = model.predict(new_data, type="link")
link_preds.values.round(3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6}
```
array([18.856, 40.992, 62.825, 75.69 ])
```
:::
:::


The difference between the two is the intercept: a single scalar added to every prediction.

::: {#bbde29f2 .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
(link_preds.values - preds_terms.values).round(4)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7}
```
array([45.2167, 45.2167, 45.2167, 45.2167])
```
:::
:::


The constant difference confirms the identity: `link prediction = intercept + sum(term contributions)`.

## Compare contributions across observations

Stack the two smooth contributions side by side to see which predictor dominates at each point.

::: {#e0cd4230 .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
np.column_stack([
    preds_terms.terms["s(age)"].round(3),
    preds_terms.terms["s(experience)"].round(3),
])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8}
```
array([[-21.521,  -4.84 ],
       [ -9.109,   4.884],
       [  5.311,  12.297],
       [ 14.86 ,  15.613]])
```
:::
:::


Rows correspond to the four observations. The first column is the `age` contribution; the second
is `experience`. When the `age` value is large and `experience` is near zero, age is the primary
driver of that prediction (and vice versa). This decomposition is more informative than inspecting
the overall fitted value alone.
